story.card_text: The local claim is big: 'the first chocolate factory in this country,' in the words of the National Register district write-up. Dr. James Baker financed it; John Hannon, an Irish immigrant, ran it. The Leventhal Map Center dates the start to 1765, in Milton, across the river, before it moved to the Dorchester side; Boston.com says 1764. Walter Baker, the grandson, gave it the name in the 1820s, and his successors gave it the Chocolate Girl. Now the correction. Boston didn't learn chocolate here. In 1670 the selectmen licensed Dorothy Jones and Jane Barnard to keep a house 'for the sellinge of Coffee and Chucalettoe.' The merchant John Hull was trading cocoa by the winter of 1667, and Boston silversmiths were making chocolate pots by about 1701. What Lower Mills had first was a water-powered mill to grind it on an industrial scale. That ran until General Foods moved production to Dover, Delaware, in 1965 - by the district's count, 188 years of chocolate in Dorchester. The mills are apartments now.

story.card_text: Everybody has a theory about the name. The popular one is Sir Isaac Newton, apple and all. The Cambridge Historical Society calls that one untrue. Fig Newtons were first made here, at the Kennedy Biscuit Company's bakery on Franklin Street, in 1891, and named after the nearby town. When the cookie turned one hundred in 1991, UPI's story named the man responsible: the plant manager, James Hazen, who was naming Kennedy's biscuits after Massachusetts cities and towns. The filling machine that made the thing possible is credited to an inventor named John Henry Mitchell. The bakery had stood here since 1869. In 1898 Kennedy merged with other bakers into the National Biscuit Company - Nabisco. The building is homes now, called the Kennedy Biscuit Lofts. When the cookie turned a hundred, Newton treated it as something to celebrate.

finale.text: That's thirteen firsts. Here's the scorecard. The telephone held up, though nobody agrees on the sentence. The safety razor didn't - two New York brothers had a patent in 1880 - but the throwaway blade did. The first public school was paid for by the rich, the first public library let you read before it let you borrow, the first chocolate factory came nearly a century after the first chocolate, and the first hotel with indoor plumbing kept the tubs in the basement. The oldest restaurant is probably old. The cake came sometime after 1865, says the hotel. Every first had someone standing behind it with a reason to say so. That's not a scandal. It's how plaques get written.

pitch_60: The French chef in the usual Boston cream pie story never existed. The hotel's own historian said so, in a comment under a recipe, in twenty nineteen. That's how this walk goes. Boston claims a lot of firsts, and Invented Here checks thirteen of them against the paperwork. The hotel called the first with indoor plumbing kept its eight bathing rooms in the basement, with their own door to the street. The oldest public school was paid for by what the town records call the richer inhabitants, not by taxes. The library that calls itself the first to lend books let people read for six weeks before it lent one. Bell's notebook says 'I want to see you,' not 'I want you.' And King Gillette didn't invent the safety razor. He invented the blade you throw away. Some firsts hold up. Most need an asterisk, and you'll be standing in front of the plaque when you find out which. It starts at Haymarket, at the oyster bar with the awning.

So the pie is real, the date isn't, and the chef is fiction. - Off the Bricks

seo.landing_copy:
Boston likes to be first. The telephone, the public school, the public library, Boston cream pie, the bargain basement, the disposable razor blade - the city has a plaque, a sign or a hotel brochure for each of them. Invented Here walks you to thirteen of those claims and then reads the paperwork.

It starts in the Blackstone Block at an oyster bar that calls itself the oldest restaurant in America, and ends on a bridge over the Fort Point Channel, looking at a razor plant that has been making blades on the water for more than a century. In between: the garret where Bell first heard sound come down a wire, the hotel that kept its bathtubs in the basement, the corner where a chef who may never have existed supposedly invented a dessert, the school Boston's richer inhabitants chipped in for, Filene's price clock, the theater Edison wired, the library that opened its reading room before it lent a book, the boarding-house sentence two men remembered two different ways, and the corner with a marker for a political monster.

Each stop is a riddle that walks you to the next corner, and the answer is something you can only get by looking: a year on an awning, a word on a plaque, a name on a marker. Then you get the story - the legend first, then what the town records, patents, landmark files and the institutions' own historians actually say. Some claims hold up. Most need an asterisk. A few are flatly wrong, and we tell you who said so.

It's about two and three-quarter hours and five kilometers, mostly flat and step-free, from Haymarket to Broadway station. There's a one-hour short cut from Government Center to the Theatre District, a bonus stop on the Common, and two T-ride side trips: the chocolate mills at Lower Mills and the Cambridgeport bakery where the Fig Newton was born.

Any two stops are free. Every fact links to its source.

story.card_text: The Union Oyster House calls itself America's oldest restaurant, and it has the stories to go with it. A future king of France lived upstairs in 1796 and taught French to pay the rent. Isaiah Thomas printed the Massachusetts Spy here. A man named Charles Forster brought the toothpick to America by paying Harvard students to ask for one. Now read the nomination that made it a National Historic Landmark in 2003. It says nobody knows when the building went up: deed research points to about 1716 or 1717, and other writers say 1704 or 1730. The Louis Philippe story is never clearly sourced. The Spy was printed here 'possibly on the third floor,' on the word of a 1961 commission report and a 1957 guidebook. The toothpick tale opens with 'tradition holds' and rests on an undated clipping. The 'oldest continually operating restaurant' line has no footnote at all. Even 1826 carries a hedge: whether the first Union Street oyster house was this one is 'likely,' the nomination says, not certain. What it does document is Hawes Atwood opening an oyster house on October 7, 1826. By the awning's count, it turned two hundred on October 7, 2026.

A man brought the toothpick to America by paying Harvard students to ask for one. Then read the nomination that made it a National Historic Landmark in two thousand three. It says nobody knows when the building went up. Deeds point to about seventeen sixteen. The king of France story is never clearly sourced. The newspaper was printed here possibly on the third floor, according to two later sources. The toothpick story starts with the words tradition holds. And the oldest restaurant line has no footnote at all. What the nomination does document is an oyster house opening on October seventh, eighteen twenty-six. story.card_text: Edward Filene worked out the idea in 1908 and opened it in 1909, in the basement of the family's old store: an Automatic Bargain Basement. Every item carried its date. According to the Boston Public Library's research guide, the price dropped by a quarter every six days, and anything still unsold after thirty days went to charity. Nobody haggled; the calendar did it. Historic New England, which holds a Filene's booklet from around 1929, catalogs it as the first off-price retailer in the United States. story.card_text: The legend says Boston gave the world the safety razor. It didn't. Frederick and Otto Kampfe of New York patented one in June 1880: a blade in a guard that cut hair, not skin. What King Gillette, a traveling salesman, came up with in 1895 was the blade itself - so thin and cheap that you'd never hone or strop it, just throw it away. His patent says exactly that. It took William Nickerson, an MIT-trained machinist, to make steel that thin hold an edge. They incorporated in 1901; Gillette filed his patent that December, and it was granted on November 15, 1904. The first year of sales, 1903, moved fifty-one razors and one hundred sixty-eight blades. By 1904 it was over ninety thousand razors. In 1905 the company bought a six-story building in South Boston, and it has made blades on this channel for more than a hundred years. Not for much longer: Procter and Gamble, which merged with Gillette in 2005, began moving razor and blade production to Andover in 2026, and the thirty-one-acre campus is slated for housing, labs and a waterfront park.
